Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using the board’s GPIO software PWM bus and four active‑low push‑buttons with internal pull‑ups, where the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), the tilt‑up button to GPIO6 (BCM), the tilt‑down button to GPIO7 (BCM), the pan‑left button to GPIO8 (BCM) and the pan‑right button to GPIO9 (BCM); the program must generate a 50 Hz PWM period (20 ms) with pulse widths ranging from 1 ms to 2 ms (corresponding to duty values of 50 to 100 out of 1000), initialize both servos to the mid‑position value 75, and on each button press adjust the corresponding axis by ±5 while clamping the position to the range 25–125, poll the button states every 50 ms, check the return status of every driver call and handle any request failures, and on receipt of SIGINT cleanly release all allocated resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi running Bookworm 64‑bit that opens the USB camera on /dev/video0, uses select() with a 2‑second timeout to wait for a frame, requests buffers, memory‑maps them, queues a buffer, starts streaming, dequeues the captured frame, stops streaming, unmaps the buffers, frees them and closes the file descriptor, handling SIGINT so that all these steps are performed cleanly on interruption; the captured image, originally in the documented YUYV format, must be converted to RGB24, processed with a blur filter, then encoded as a JPEG file named capture_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.jpg with quality set to 75, and every system call and memory allocation must be checked for failure with error messages printed to stderr and all resources released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi running a 32‑bit or 64‑bit kernel with the V4L2 subsystem active that opens the CSI camera device node /dev/video0, checks that the node exists and can be opened, queries the device capabilities with VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, enumerates all supported frame sizes using VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMESIZES and for each size enumerates the available frame intervals with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMEINTERVALS, then queries the V4L2_CID_FOCUS_AUTO control with VIDIOC_QUERYCTRL to determine whether autofocus is supported, printing a clear, human‑readable summary of the resolutions, frame rates and autofocus capability to stdout; the program must verify every ioctl return value, handle the cases where the device node is missing, cannot be opened, the camera does not support frame‑size or interval enumeration, or the focus control is absent, and exit with a non‑zero status on any fatal error.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using two hobby servos driven over the GPIO hardware PWM bus, with four active‑low push‑buttons wired to ground and using the internal pull‑up resistors; the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), while the UP, DOWN, LEFT and RIGHT buttons are on GPIO6, GPIO7, GPIO8 and GPIO9 respectively, all using 50 Hz PWM where each loop iteration increments the pulse width by 10 µs and the loop delays 50 ms, the pulse widths must be clamped between 1000 µs (minimum) and 2000 µs (maximum) with a center position of 1500 µs, the program must initialize the driver library and check its return value, printing an error and exiting if initialization fails, output a startup message showing the pin assignments and the center position, respond to button presses by adjusting the appropriate servo pulse width in the allowed range, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly stops PWM on both servo pins using the library's API call, calls the library's API call() to release resources, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor connected on the GPIO bus with its output tied to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11), debounces each motion detection for two seconds, and otherwise polls the pin every 100 ms; when motion is detected the program must capture a JPEG snapshot from the Camera Module v2 at quality 85, store the file in a directory named motion_captures (creating the directory if necessary and handling an existing directory gracefully), then compose a JSON payload containing the filename, an ISO 8601 timestamp with microseconds, the motion status, and the GPIO pin number and POST this payload together with the image to an HTTP endpoint at http://<IP>:<port>/upload, where the IP address and port are supplied as command‑line arguments; the program must initialize the sensor driver and the HTTP library, configure GPIO17 as an input with a pull‑down resistor, check and report any initialization, system call, file, or network errors to stderr, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a clean shutdown by releasing the driver, performing the required global cleanup of the HTTP library, and exiting, while ensuring the global HTTP library initialization is called exactly once at startup and the corresponding cleanup is called exactly once at exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that monitors the HC‑SR501 PIR sensor on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s output connected to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) as an input with edge‑falling detection, implements a 50 ms debounce by waiting for a falling edge with a timeout, and upon a valid motion event invokes the camera capture utility with the options ‑o <filename> ‑‑width 640 ‑‑height 480 ‑q 85 ‑‑timeout 2000 ‑‑nopreview to produce a timestamped JPEG saved in /home/pi/images using the filename format YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_mmm.jpg; each capture and any error from the capture command must be logged with a timestamp to /home/pi/motion_capture.log; the program must open the GPIO chip, claim GPIO17 as an input with edge‑falling (or edge‑rising) detection, check return codes of the capture command and log failures, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing all driver library resources and closing file descriptors, while assuming the images directory already exists and avoiding any network publishing, ZeroMQ, or use of a driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (32‑bit or 64‑bit) that opens the USB UVC camera on /dev/video0, uses VIDIOC_QUERYCAP to verify the device, configures the capture to the documented V4L2_PIX_FMT_YUYV with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, requests a single memory‑mapped buffer, starts streaming, and then uses select() with a 2‑second timeout (retrying ioctl calls on EINTR) to wait for a frame; after a successful capture it must check that the returned width, height and pixel format match the requested values before processing, copy the complete YUYV macroblocks (Y0,U,Y1,V) to avoid color corruption, crop a 200 × 150 region, and write exactly 200*150*2 bytes to a file named cropped.yuv, checking the return value of every syscall, ioctl, mmap, fopen and fwrite and printing any errno with perror followed by EXIT_FAILURE on error; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must cleanly stop streaming, unmap the buffer, close the file descriptor and free any allocated memory.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads arrow‑key presses and a ‘q’ character from stdin, uses the GPIO hardware PWM bus to drive two SG90 servo motors—one pan servo attached to GPIO17 (BCM) and one tilt servo attached to GPIO18 (BCM)—operating at a 50 Hz frequency, initializing the driver library and exiting with code 1 after printing an error if initialization fails, starting both servos at a neutral 90‑degree position, moving each servo in 5‑degree steps in response to the appropriate arrow key while enforcing angle limits of 0 to 180 degrees and printing clear error messages for any out‑of‑range angle or PWM failure, inserting a 100 ms delay between successive commands, and handling cleanup by setting both servos to neutral, terminating the driver library cleanly, and exiting when a SIGINT signal is received or the user presses ‘q’.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and parses the CPU usage percentage from /proc/stat, then renders both values once per second on an SSD1306 128×64 I2C OLED display attached to I2C bus 1, using a basic 5×7 bitmap font for text; the program must check every I2C write operation for errors, handle file‑read failures by returning specific error strings to be shown on the OLED, log any I2C communication failures to stderr and exit gracefully, and install a SIGINT handler to cleanly release all resources before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the pulse output of a YF‑S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), computes the instantaneous flow rate and accumulates total volume, logs the current flow rate and total volume to the console once every second, and updates an HD44780 LCD attached via I2C bus 1 every ten seconds to display the same current flow rate and accumulated volume; the implementation must include robust error handling for any failures during GPIO initialization and must anticipate and manage possible I2C communication errors, and it must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO and I2C resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads an anemometer pulse on GPIO17 (BCM) using an interrupt on the rising edge, counts pulses over a 500 ms sample window to compute real‑time wind speed, and reads wind direction from a wind vane connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0/CE0 in mode 0 at 1 MHz; the program must then update a 16x2 LCD with a PCF8574 backpack on I2C bus 1 to display both wind speed and direction every 500 ms, checking the result of every driver library, I2C and SPI call, detecting sensor‑absent conditions such as the ADC reading stuck at 0 or 1023 or any I2C/SPI failures and printing diagnostic messages to stderr while continuing to run, and finally handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases the SPI handle, the I2C handle and any driver library resources, using the provided driver library’s I2C and SPI bit‑bang helpers or direct /dev/i2c and /dev/spidev access via its spi0SPIOpen call where appropriate.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that measures water flow rate using a single YF‑S201 water flow sensor whose pulse output is connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) and displays the result on an LCD1602 attached via I2C bus 1; the program must count sensor pulses over a 1‑second interval to compute the flow in liters per minute and show “Flow Rate:” on the first line of the LCD and the calculated value formatted as “X.XX L/min” on the second line, while providing robust error handling for driver library initialization, GPIO mode and alert setup, and any I2C bus open or write failures, also detecting and handling sensor‑absent conditions such as zero pulses for extended periods, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path and perform a graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that drives an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix over the GPIO bus, using the row anodes on GPIO 17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM) and the column cathodes on GPIO 5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20 (BCM), scanning each row with an 800 µs delay, lighting an LED by setting the corresponding row HIGH and column LOW, and rendering two wave‑like animations that shift each frame, one moving left‑to‑right and the other right‑to‑left; the program must check every driver call, print descriptive error messages to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status on failure, and must handle a graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing all GPIO lines and performing cleanup, while adhering to the constraint of not using any driver library or deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that creates a wave‑like animation on an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix driven directly over GPIO, with the row anodes connected to GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 (BCM) and the column cathodes to GPIO 14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 (BCM); the program must scan the columns left to right, clearing the matrix before each column by setting all column cathodes HIGH and all row anodes LOW, then for each column set the column cathode LOW and light the LEDs sequentially by setting the corresponding row anodes HIGH, observing a 150 ms delay between columns, checking the result of every GPIO operation and handling a chip‑open failure, using the driver library v2 API for all GPIO calls, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly releases all GPIO lines on exit, while respecting the hardware constraint that each column cathode is wired through a current‑limiting resistor (e.g., 220 Ω) and that a column lights when its cathode is LOW and all row anodes are HIGH, and the program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads distance measurements for multiple targets from an STMicroelectronics VL53L3CX Time‑of‑Flight multi‑target sensor connected on I2C bus 1, polling the sensor every 100 ms and printing to the console ISO‑8601 timestamped distance values for all detected targets; the program must verify the sensor model ID during initialization, perform the required complex proprietary initialization sequence (or clearly stub the proprietary firmware download with a descriptive comment while keeping the I2C communication and error handling fully implemented), check every I2C read/write return code and handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads distance data from a Melexis MLX75031 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, samples the sensor every 100 ms, and appends each reading to a file named depth_log.csv, creating a CSV header row if the file is newly created and writing timestamped distance values; the program must verify successful initialization of the sensor interface, opening of the I2C bus, each I2C read/write transaction, and all file operations, and if an I2C read fails it must log a row with distance ‑1, attempt to re‑open the I2C handle, and continue sampling, while also handling SIGINT to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates the sensor interface without using any driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads proximity and ambient‑light data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 proximity/ambient‑light sensor attached to I2C bus 1, sampling every 500 ms, and appends each reading to a file named biometric_log.txt prefixed with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; the program must handle I2C read failures gracefully by logging the error and continuing, and if the sensor is absent or initialization fails it must print a diagnostic message to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status, while also installing a SIGINT handler that, upon receipt, cleanly closes the I2C handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls the sensor’s library API call() before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously polls an E18‑D50NK IR proximity sensor connected to GPIO line 4 (BCM, physical pin 7) every 100 ms, reads the sensor which drives the line LOW when an object is within the calibrated range and HIGH otherwise, and detects the falling edge from HIGH to LOW so that a timestamped entry is written only once per detection to a file named proximity.log using an ISO 8601 UTC format such as “2024-01-15T12:34:56Z Object detected”; when a detection occurs the program must also blink an LED attached to GPIO line 17 (BCM, physical pin 11) by turning it on for 100 ms and then off, and it must check the return status of every driver call, handle any file‑I/O errors, and on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—release the GPIO lines and close the chip, opening the GPIO chip first with the library’s API call that takes the default chip name and, if that fails, falling back to the library’s API call with the string “the library’s API call”, never invoking the API without arguments.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads proximity and ambient light data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor attached to I2C bus 1, first verifying the sensor’s PART_ID before entering an infinite loop that samples the two measurements once per second, and logs each reading to a file named biometric_data.log in CSV format with an ISO‑8601 timestamp followed by the proximity value and the ambient light value, flushing the file after every write; the program must check the return code of every I2C read and write operation, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors in a graceful manner, and install a SIGINT handler that, upon termination, closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and calls the sensor’s API call() function for proper cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that drives an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor over GPIO, using GPIO 17 (BCM) as the TRIGGER output and GPIO 27 (BCM) as the ECHO input, with a 1 kΩ/2 kΩ voltage divider on the echo line to protect the 3.3 V‑tolerant pins from the sensor’s 5 V logic; the program must issue a 10 µs trigger pulse, then wait up to 30 ms for the echo rise and up to another 30 ms for the echo pulse width, compute the distance, reject any reading outside the 2‑400 cm range, and every 60 seconds log the result to a file named distance_log.txt with an ISO‑8601 timestamp, including explicit error or timeout entries, and if the measured distance is below 15 cm also log the message “Time to water the plant!”; all driver calls must be checked for failure, handling the sensor‑absent case where the echo never rises and the timeout case where the echo stays high, and the application must catch SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all resources and closes the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Adafruit APDS9960 sensor on I2C bus 1 to poll the device every 100 ms, detect proximity events and read the raw RGB color values, and whenever the proximity reading exceeds the threshold of 200 it appends a line containing the timestamp, the three RGB components and the proximity value to a CSV file named color_proximity_log.csv; the program must handle I2C communication errors by closing and reopening the bus and re‑initializing the sensor, and it must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, finalizes the CSV file, and releases any resources allocated by the driver.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that communicates with a Silicon Labs Si1182‑A‑GMR optical sensor over I2C (/dev/i2c‑1) to measure heart rate, reading the proximity data registers every 100 ms, converting each reading to beats‑per‑minute, and appending a line to a file named heartrate.csv in the form “timestamp,bpm” where the timestamp is an ISO‑8601 string; after each write the program must call fflush, and every i2c_smbus_* call must be checked for errors, aborting the program on any initialization failure but, if a read fails during the loop, printing a warning to stderr, skipping that sample and continuing; the application must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile running = false flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, after which it closes the I2C file descriptor, closes the CSV file and returns 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to communicate with an Adafruit VL53L0X Time‑of‑Flight sensor, first verifying the sensor’s presence at the documented value before any initialization, then configuring a falling‑edge trigger input on GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) with a pull‑up resistor; the program must wait for each falling edge, trigger a single distance measurement, poll the RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS with approximately a 100 ms timeout, and upon successful read log a timestamped distance in millimetres to a file named distance_log.txt in CSV format as “timestamp,distance_mm”, while providing robust error handling for every I2C transaction, handling sensor‑absent conditions and timeout paths, and must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt performs a graceful shutdown by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and releasing all driver library resources on every exit path, all without using the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the TDK CH101 ultrasonic sensor on I2C bus 1 to measure distance, waiting approximately 50 ms after each trigger before reading the result and sampling every 200 ms; the program must initialize the driver and open the I2C bus, verify each write and read operation as well as the file open for logging, and on any I2C error print a diagnostic message and skip to the next sample without crashing, while logging each successful reading in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, <distance_mm>” to a file named distance_log.txt and also printing the same line to stdout, using a fixed‑size local buffer for the timestamp to avoid dynamic allocation, and it must handle SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) gracefully by exiting the sampling loop, closing the I2C handle, the log file, and shutting down the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Silicon Labs Si1102 proximity sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, configures the sensor’s proximity interrupt to GPIO27 (BCM numbering) on a rising edge, and on each interrupt reads the 16‑bit proximity value, compares it to a threshold (default 1000 but overrideable with a command‑line option “‑t <threshold>”), and appends a line to a file named proximity.log containing the current timestamp in “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” format, the raw proximity reading, and the status string “SAFE” if the value is less than or equal to the threshold or “ALERT” if it exceeds the threshold; the program must also accept an optional “‑a <i2c_address>” argument to set the I2C address in hex or decimal, must initialise the I2C interface and GPIO with full error checking, must verify every I2C transaction, GPIO setup, and file operation and print any errors to stderr, must implement a thread‑safe interrupt handler that does not perform blocking calls (using a flag or queue to defer processing), and must install a SIGINT handler that on receipt cleanly shuts down by closing the I2C device, closing the log file, and terminating the sensor driver, while using the provided driver facilities for GPIO and I2C but not for higher‑level sensor handling.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses an interrupt‑driven HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor to measure distance and activates a buzzer when the measured distance falls below 20 cm, configuring GPIO17 (BCM) as the trigger output, GPIO18 (BCM) as the echo input with a rising/falling edge alert callback, and GPIO27 (BCM) as the buzzer output; the program must generate a 10 µs trigger pulse, measure the echo pulse width in an interrupt handler by recording timestamps on both edges, compute the distance, print the distance to stdout every second, set the buzzer pin high if the distance is under 20 cm otherwise set it low, initialise the driver library and verify its success, check every driver library call and report any failure to stderr, and install a SIGINT handler that cleanly terminates the driver library and exits, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously implements a parking‑assist system by measuring distance with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected with its trigger pin on GPIO4 (BCM) and echo pin on GPIO17 (BCM), displaying the measured distance in centimeters on the console, and rotating an SG90 servo motor on GPIO18 (BCM) using the library’s API call so that the servo angle is proportional to the distance—0° (500 µs pulse) at 200 cm, 90° (1500 µs pulse) at 110 cm, and 180° (2500 µs pulse) at 20 cm—updating both the distance reading and the servo angle every 100 ms, checking that the driver library initializes correctly, handling echo timeouts by returning –1.0 and retrying on sensor errors, and installing a SIGINT handler that on interruption stops the library’s API call, terminates the driver library, and exits cleanly, while using the library’s API for timing rather than busy‑wait loops and running continuously until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that communicates with a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 using the sensor’s default address, verifies the documented model ID at the documented register, programs the documented timing budget, and starts ranging; the program must repeatedly poll the 16‑bit distance register, and based on the measured distance operate a servo‑actuated gate connected to GPIO18 (BCM, hardware PWM‑capable) by setting a 1000 µs pulse width when the object is farther than 250 mm and a 2000 µs pulse width when it is closer than 200 mm, thereby providing hysteresis, while smoothing the transition between these pulse widths; every time the gate opens or closes the event must be written with a timestamp to a file named gate_log.txt, I2C read/write errors must be handled gracefully, and on receipt of SIGINT the program must cleanly release the I2C handle, shut down the driver, stop the PWM and close the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously measures the distance to an object with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected with the trigger line on GPIO23 (BCM) and the echo line on GPIO24 (BCM), issuing a 10 µs trigger pulse and waiting up to a 50 ms timeout for both the rising and falling edges, then pausing 100 ms before the next measurement, and maps the measured distance (valid from 2 cm to 400 cm) to a servo angle using an SG90 servo attached to GPIO18 (BCM, powered from 5 V with a common ground) by calling the provided API to set pulse widths of 500 µs for 0° and 2500 µs for 180°, where distances below 20 cm correspond to 0°, distances above 200 cm correspond to 180°, and intermediate values are linearly interpolated; each cycle the program must print the distance and the corresponding angle, initialise the driver with error checking and exit with a clear message if initialisation fails, verify the return of every API call, treat a timeout from the sensor as a distance of –1.0, guard against division by zero or invalid angles, and install a SIGINT handler that stops the servo by sending a 0‑degree command through the API and cleanly shuts down the driver before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Silicon Labs Si7005 humidity and temperature sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented device address, verifies successful initialization of the driver library and opening of the I2C bus, and then repeatedly reads the sensor by first writing the CONFIG register, waiting 10 ms, writing the register address to be read, waiting another 10 ms for conversion, and finally performing the I2C read; each successful read must be logged to the console every 2 seconds, while every I2C read or write operation must be checked for errors and, on any failure, the program must close and re‑open the I2C handle to attempt recovery, and the application must handle SIGINT to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle and terminates the driver library on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads raw accelerometer and gyroscope data from a TDK InvenSense MPU‑6050 over I2C bus 1 (SDA on GPIO2 BCM, SCL on GPIO3 BCM) and logs it to the console, beginning with a brief startup message and ending with a clean‑shutdown message; the program must first verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register, then every 100 ms read the 14‑byte data block starting at the documented register using the library’s API call, parse the big‑endian int16 values for the three‑axis accelerometer, temperature and three‑axis gyroscope, and print those values to stdout each cycle, while handling any I2C read/write errors or sensor‑absent conditions, and must catch SIGINT or SIGTERM to close the I2C handle and invoke the library’s API call for cleanup before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads temperature and humidity from an Adafruit SHT40 I2C sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented sensor address, triggers a high‑repeatability measurement by sending the documented command, waits at least 10 ms, then reads the six‑byte response (two bytes temperature, one CRC, two bytes humidity, one CRC) and validates both CRC‑8 checksums with the documented polynomial and initial value; the program must log the temperature and humidity readings to the console every 5 seconds, and on any I2C read/write error or CRC failure it must print a diagnostic message to stderr and re‑open the I2C bus before the next attempt, while also handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle and terminates the driver library on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads ambient and object temperatures from a Melexis MLX90614ESF-BAA infrared temperature sensor over the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 using the sensor’s default address, performs a read every 5 seconds, and appends each reading together with a timestamp to a comma‑separated file named temperature_log.csv; the program must handle I2C initialisation failures, sensor‑absent scenarios such as read errors, and file I/O errors in a graceful manner, and it must also catch SIGINT to cleanly release resources by closing the I2C file descriptor and the log file, all within the constraints of a contactless food safety monitoring system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically samples temperature from a Sensirion STS30-DIS temperature‑only sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, taking a reading every 5 seconds, and appends each timestamped temperature value to a file named enclosure_temp_log.txt while implementing robust error handling for any I2C communication failures—including cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors—and logging all such error messages to a separate file called error_log.txt; the program must also ensure clean release of all resources on every exit path and must handle termination signals such as Ctrl+C to perform the same orderly cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously measures differential pressure and temperature from the Sensirion SDP810‑125Pa differential pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, configuring the sensor for continuous measurement by sending the documented command bytes, then every second issuing the measurement command, waiting at least 1 ms before reading the 9‑byte data frame that contains the differential pressure (2 bytes plus CRC‑8), temperature (2 bytes plus CRC‑8) and their respective scale factors (2 bytes plus CRC‑8), validating each CRC‑8 with the documented polynomial and initialization value, converting the raw values with the received scale factors, and appending a line to a comma‑separated file named pressure_log.csv that includes an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, the pressure in pascals and the temperature in degrees Celsius, creating a header row if the file is new; the program must check all driver and file I/O operations for errors, handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with a Sensirion SHT40 humidity and temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 using the SDA pin on GPIO2 (BCM) and the SCL pin on GPIO3 (BCM) at the documented 7‑bit address, issuing the high‑repeatability measurement command (documented value) and then waiting at least 10 ms before reading the 6‑byte result (two bytes temperature MSB+LSB, one CRC, two bytes humidity MSB+LSB, one CRC), validating each reading with the Sensirion CRC‑8 algorithm using the documented polynomial and initial value, and logging timestamped temperature and humidity values to a file named ‘sht40_log.txt’ every 5 seconds; the program must robustly handle errors from opening the I2C device, ioctl calls, writes, and reads by logging an error and retrying on the next cycle, and it must cleanly close both the I2C file descriptor and the log file when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP31 (±500 Pa) differential pressure sensor on I²C bus 1 using the documented I²C address, triggers continuous measurement with the documented command, waits at least 1 ms after the trigger, then reads the six‑byte response (pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC), converts the values to pressure in pascals and temperature in degrees Celsius, and appends a line containing a timestamp, pressure_pa and temperature_c as comma‑separated fields to a file named airflow.log, flushing the file after each write; the sampling interval must be 100 ms, and any I²C write or read failure must be retried up to three times with exponential backoff, using the driver library functions for all sensor interactions, while handling SIGINT and SIGTERM via a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, and on every exit path the program must close the I²C handle, close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API call().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads temperature and humidity from a Silicon Labs Si7015 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, operates the sensor in No Hold Master mode by writing the documented command for temperature or humidity and then polling‑reading the two‑byte result until the measurement is ready (taking no more than about 20 ms per measurement), samples the data every 5 seconds, and logs each reading together with a timestamp to a file named sensor_data.txt opened in append mode while also printing the timestamped values to the console; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, opening of the I2C bus, each I2C write and read operation, and opening of the log file, retry transient I2C failures, and terminate cleanly with an error message if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs, and it must handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by closing the I2C handle, terminating the driver library, and closing any open file before exiting, using <errno.h> for strerror() as needed.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that configures I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 pressure sensor, validates the calibration data read from the documented registers before any measurement, and then uses a hardware timer interrupt to trigger a sample every 500 ms, reading temperature in degrees Celsius and pressure in pascals with the oversampling setting set to 0 (ultra low power) and appending the results to a file named bmp180_log.txt; the implementation must include robust error handling for all I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, and read/write timeouts, and must ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the CPU temperature from the thermal zone file /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, maps the temperature linearly to a PWM duty cycle on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 25 kHz frequency and a 0‑255 range such that 40 °C corresponds to 0 % duty, 70 °C to 100 % duty and values are clamped below 40 °C and above 70 °C, drives a PWM‑controlled cooling fan accordingly, logs every 5 seconds to a file named fan_log.txt the current timestamp, temperature and duty cycle, and includes robust error handling for failures to read the temperature, write to the log file, or initialize the PWM driver, while also installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully stop the fan, close any open files and terminate the PWM driver before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA on GPIO2 pin 3, SCL on GPIO3 pin 5) using the documented default address when SDO is tied to GND and falling back to the documented alternative address, applies the Bosch 64‑bit compensation formulas, rewrites the ctrl_meas register in forced mode each loop to trigger a new measurement, and appends a line to weather_data.txt every five seconds in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa”, while checking every I/O call (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs) for errors, logging any sensor I/O failures to stderr and attempting to continue or exit gracefully, ensuring the sensor is powered from the 3.3 V rail only, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to break the logging loop, close the I2C file descriptor and any open files, and exit with status 0.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the temperature from an LM75 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, performs the read once per second, stores each reading in an in‑memory circular buffer of capacity 60 samples protected by a mutex, updates a running average from the buffer, and drives an alert LED connected to GPIO18 (BCM) from a background thread so that the LED is turned on whenever the temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off otherwise; the implementation must check the result of every I2C read/write and every GPIO initialization call, log any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions to stderr, attempt to re‑initialize the hardware on such errors, and ensure that on all exit paths—including normal termination, error paths, and receipt of SIGINT—the program cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C file descriptor, releasing the GPIO line, and destroying the mutex.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a BMP180 sensor on the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1, sampling once per second, and writes any temperature reading above 30.0 °C or pressure reading below 950 hPa to a file named breach_log.txt with a timestamp for each breach; the program must perform all BMP180 calibration calculations using integer arithmetic only, avoid any floating‑point pow operations, check the result of every system call and retry transient failures up to three times, explicitly handle cases where the sensor is absent or the I2C bus reports an error, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples a BMP180 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, reading and validating the 11‑word calibration table from the documented register before any sampling, and then, via a hardware timer callback that fires every 500 ms, obtains temperature and pressure using the BMP180 formulas with OSS = 0 (ensuring the temperature routine is not called from inside the pressure routine), stores each timestamped reading in a 60‑entry circular buffer, prints each new reading to stdout, and drives a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (active‑high) whenever the temperature exceeds 30 °C; the timer callback must remain simple and avoid blocking calls, every library API call’s return code must be checked and the sample skipped on error, and the program must handle SIGINT/SIGTERM by turning the fan off, closing the I2C handle, and invoking the library’s cleanup API call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces to a BMP180 sensor on the I2C bus using the documented address, reads the sensor’s calibration data and applies the Bosch compensation formulas to compute pressure in pascals, and toggles data logging on and off via a falling‑edge interrupt on GPIO27 with a 200 ms debounce; while logging is enabled the program must record a timestamp and the computed pressure to a file named pressure_log.txt every 2 seconds, must detect and recover from I2C communication errors and driver initialization failures, and must clean up all allocated resources and gracefully terminate when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier on SPI0 using CE0 (GPIO8 as chip‑select, GPIO9 MISO, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO11 SCLK) at 2 MHz, drives a solid‑state relay connected to GPIO17 with a PWM signal to modulate a resistive heater so that a PI controller with anti‑windup maintains a target temperature (default 25.0 °C) while never exceeding a safe maximum duty cycle of 80 %, logs each measurement and the applied duty cycle together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named heater_log.csv, and implements error handling such that any SPI read failure or any MAX31855 fault condition (open circuit, short to ground or VCC) causes the duty cycle to be set immediately to 0 % and the error to be recorded in the log while the program continues running, and also catches SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off the heater, closes the SPI interface, closes the log file, and terminates the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the CPU temperature every 0.5 seconds and drives a common‑anode RGB LED attached to the GPIO bus with the Red cathode on GPIO17, Green cathode on GPIO18 and Blue cathode on GPIO27, using hardware PWM via the library’s API call() with a 0‑255 range and inverted duty (255 turns the channel off) while respecting the 3.3 V common‑anode supply and individual current‑limiting resistors; the program must open the temperature file, check the return value of the API call() each time it sets a PWM value and on any failure print an error message and exit with a non‑zero status, also handling fopen failure and short or failed reads by checking ferror, printing a diagnostic and skipping that update cycle, and on each loop iteration print to stdout the temperature in millidegrees Celsius together with the three PWM values; the LED color should be solid Blue (0,0,255) for temperatures below 40000 m°C, solid Green (0,255,0) for 40000‑59999 m°C, and solid Red (255,0,0) for 60000 m°C and above; a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, turn off all channels by writing a duty of 255, call the library’s API call() for cleanup, and allow the main loop to exit gracefully without calling exit() inside the handler, ensuring the file handle is closed on every code path and the program runs an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity and temperature from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus with its data line on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), using the required start signal of pulling the line low for at least 1 ms, then captures the full 40‑bit response, validates the 8‑bit checksum, and posts the measured values as a JSON payload to http://yourserver.com/api/humidity via HTTP; the implementation must gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent, checksum mismatches, and network errors by retrying up to three times, and must ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 sensor, configuring the sensor for oversampling setting OSS=3 and applying the full Bosch BMP180 integer‑only compensation algorithm, and that toggles data logging on and off with a push‑button connected to GPIO 4 configured for falling‑edge interrupts with the internal pull‑up; the interrupt handler must debounce using a driver‑library tick comparison of at least 200 000 µs, and when logging is enabled the program shall read pressure every 2 seconds, waiting the required 26 ms conversion delay, and append a timestamped pressure value in hPa to a file named pressure_log.txt, while printing a status message when logging is disabled; the code must check every I2C read/write return value, report any errors to stderr, fail cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid calibration data, and on receipt of SIGINT must close the I2C handle and release all driver resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus using GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) by issuing the start signal (pull the data line low for at least 1 ms, then high for 20‑40 µs, then release), captures the 40‑bit response with microsecond‑level edge timing, validates the checksum and, if the sensor is absent or the checksum fails, retries up to three times with a 2‑second backoff before giving up; the main loop must perform a read every 10 seconds, and each successful reading must be formatted as JSON and POSTed with Content‑Type: application/json to http://your‑the‑library’s‑API‑call.com/api/humidity, retrying the POST up to three times on network or HTTP errors and treating any non‑2xx response as a failure; the program must initialize the driver library with the library’s API call() and check for errors, log all events to syslog, accept a command‑line option “-s <url>” to override the default URL, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that calls the library’s API call() and curl_global_cleanup() on every exit path.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors a Keyes KY-026 Flame Sensor connected via the GPIO bus, with the sensor’s digital output (DO) wired to GPIO17 (Broadcom pin 17, physical pin 11) configured as an input with an internal pull‑up, and polls the line every 100 ms to detect a falling‑edge event (the transition from HIGH to LOW, since the sensor is active‑low: LOW indicates a flame); on each detected falling edge the program must print “FLAME DETECTED” to the console and append a timestamped “FLAME DETECTED” line to a file named flame_log.txt opened in append mode with an immediate flush, while ensuring that duplicate alerts are not generated while the line remains low; every driver library call and file operation must be checked for errors, and the code must handle the situation where the GPIO chip or the specific line is unavailable; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must be installed to perform graceful shutdown on all exit paths by releasing the GPIO line, closing the GPIO chip, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the GPIO bus to read an 8‑channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module connected on BCM pins 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 (OUT1‑OUT8) and drives an 8‑bit binary counter on GPIO 17 through GPIO 24 (bit 0 on 17, bit 7 on 24), polling the sensor lines every 10 ms after an initial 200 ms stabilization delay; on each rising edge (idle 0 V to touched 3.3 V) the program must increment the counter, wrapping from 255 to 0, immediately update the eight output pins via the driver’s bulk/config API calls, and log the event to a file named touch_log.txt in append mode using an ISO‑8601 UTC timestamp “YYYY‑MM‑DDTHH:MM:SSZ, Channel: <1‑8>, Counter: <0‑255>” while also printing to stdout “Touch on channel <N> | Counter: <V>”, checking every driver call, file open and I/O operation and reporting errors with strerror(errno); if any line request fails the program must clean up all previously acquired resources and exit non‑zero, if a driver API call fails it must print the error and exit non‑zero, if a sensor read returns an error it must log the error to stderr and skip that channel for the iteration, if an output write fails it must log the error to stderr but continue, and if opening the log file fails it must warn on stderr yet keep stdout output functional; finally the program must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by resetting all output pins to 0, releasing all driver resources, closing the chip and exiting with status 0, and it must be built with gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o touch_counter touch_counter.c -lgpiod.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that polls four Keywish KY-033 4‑Way Infrared Tracking Module sensors connected via GPIO—sensor 1 on GPIO17 (BCM), sensor 2 on GPIO18 (BCM), sensor 3 on GPIO27 (BCM), and sensor 4 on GPIO22 (BCM)—every 100 ms, reading each active‑low output (0 indicates line or obstacle detected, 1 indicates no line), and appends a row to a timestamped CSV file named tracking_log.csv with columns timestamp,sensor1,sensor2,sensor3,sensor4, writing a header row if the file does not yet exist; the program must robustly check every initialization and read call, printing clear error messages to stderr and continuing when possible if a GPIO request or read fails, must use the modern driver library API calls for GPIO handling, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources, closes and flushes the CSV file after each write to prevent data loss on abrupt termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that monitors two Omron D7E‑5 tilt sensors connected on the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) and sensor 2 to GPIO18 (BCM, physical pin 12), configuring both lines as inputs with an active‑low pull‑up (BiasPullUp) so that an unconnected sensor reads high and a tilt event pulls the line low; the program must poll both lines every 100 ms and use a 50 ms debounce window to detect edges, logging only transitions from inactive (1) to active (0) by appending a timestamped entry to /var/log/tilt_events.log in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Sensor X tilted\n” where X is 1 for GPIO17 and 2 for GPIO18, handling chip open failure, line request failure, and read errors by printing an error message to stderr and either exiting or continuing gracefully as appropriate, and installing handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that release all driver resources (chip and lines) and close the log file cleanly before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads reflectance data from two TCRT5000 IR obstacle‑avoidance sensor modules connected on the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO27 (BCM), and drives an LED on GPIO22 (BCM); the program must poll both sensors every 100 ms, treat the sensors as active‑low (0 indicates an obstacle, 1 indicates clear), turn the LED high only when both sensors read 0, and log each sample to a file named obstacle_log.csv using the column order timestamp,sensor1,sensor2,led_state, flushing the file after every write; it must check the result of every driver library C‑API call, handle the situation where any API call is unavailable, verify that the log file opens successfully, and on receiving a SIGINT perform a graceful shutdown by turning the LED off, releasing all line resources, closing the chip, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously samples the analog output of a TDK InvenSense ICS‑40180 analog MEMS microphone connected to GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) by polling the pin as a digital input at roughly 8 kHz (a 125 µs period) using the provided library’s API call, treats any HIGH reading as a sound‑peak event, prints a millisecond‑precision timestamp to stdout for each detected peak, and for each peak turns on an LED wired with an appropriate current‑limiting resistor on GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) for exactly 100 ms; the program must check the return value of every library API call and report any errors to stderr, employ a volatile sig_atomic_t flag to catch SIGINT, and on receiving that signal cleanly stop the sampling loop, ensure the LED is turned OFF, and invoke the library’s shutdown API call, while never calling any library functions directly from within the signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the left, center, and right IR reflectance states from a SunFounder 3‑Way Tracing Sensor connected via the GPIO bus, with the left sensor on GPIO17 (BCM), the center sensor on GPIO27 (BCM), and the right sensor on GPIO22 (BCM), configuring each pin as an active‑low input with an internal pull‑up resistor, and logs the three sensor states to the console every 100 ms while providing robust error handling for any GPIO initialization failures, line request failures, or read errors, and ensures clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the visible ambient light sensor (ALS) data from a Silicon Labs Si1175 optical heart‑rate sensor on I2C bus 1 at fixed 100 ms intervals, combines the LSB and MSB registers into a single 16‑bit raw value, and logs each raw sensor reading to the console, while providing robust error handling for I2C initialization failures, read errors, sensor‑absent conditions, and bus‑error paths, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of a Ctrl +C signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that polls three Keywish 3‑Way Tracking Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO) lines on the GPIO bus—left on GPIO2 (BCM), middle on GPIO3 (BCM) and right on GPIO4 (BCM)—every 100 ms, reads each digital value using separate driver calls, checks the result of every driver call (opening the device, getting each line, requesting each line, reading each line) and handles errors such as the device being absent or permission‑denied, then logs the sensor values to stdout in the exact format “L:<0|1> M:<0|1> R:<0|1>”, and ensures that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by installing a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) handler that terminates the program gracefully while still using only individual API calls rather than any bulk interface to maximize portability across driver versions.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus with hardware PWM at 1000 Hz and an 8‑bit range to smoothly fade a common‑anode RGB LED (Red on GPIO17 (BCM), Green on GPIO18 (BCM), Blue on GPIO27 (BCM)) between randomly chosen hues, selecting each new hue internally with rand() seeded from /dev/urandom, and performing a 50‑step linear interpolation over a 5‑second interval for each transition while clamping all channel values to the 0‑255 range; the program must verify the driver library initialization and check the return value of every library API call, logging any errors via syslog, and it must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully shut down by turning off the LED, releasing the driver resources, and closing syslog, with no networking or external message bus involved.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the ambient light level from a BH1750 I2C light sensor on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1), waiting approximately 120 ms after initiating a conversion before reading the 2‑byte result, and then scales the brightness of an APA102 LED strip connected via the SPI bus (/dev/spidev0.0) proportionally to the measured illumination; the APA102 data stream must be constructed with a 32‑bit zero start frame, followed by one 32‑bit LED frame per LED containing the documented brightness, blue, green, and red fields, and terminated with a 32‑bit end frame, transmitted at a 1 MHz SPI clock, while implementing robust error handling for all I/O operations, sensor‑absent scenarios, and bus errors, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT the program gracefully turns off all LEDs and closes every opened file descriptor.
pinned_library: Linux i2c-dev and spidev character devices

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads ambient light from up to three BH1750 I2C light sensors on I2C bus 1, averaging the valid readings, and uses the result to smoothly adjust the global brightness of an APA102 RGB LED strip driven over hardware SPI, with the APA102 data line (MOSI) connected to GPIO10 (BCM) and the clock line (SCLK) to GPIO11 (BCM); the program must wait approximately 180 ms after initiating a conversion before reading the two‑byte result from each sensor, attempt to open both possible BH1750 addresses and gracefully skip any sensor that is not present, check all driver initialization and I2C/SPI calls for errors and handle missing sensors or bus errors without crashing, fade the strip’s brightness to the newly computed target over 500 ms, loop indefinitely with a 100 ms delay between cycles, and install a SIGINT handler that on termination turns off the LED strip, closes all I2C handles, closes the SPI handle, and terminates the driver library on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads ambient light from a VEML7700 ambient light sensor on the I2C bus, applies gamma‑corrected scaling to determine a brightness level for a WS2812B LED strip, and drives the strip by bit‑banging the data line on GPIO18 (BCM) without using any deprecated or external driver libraries, toggling at the required high frequency (approximately 800 kHz) or falling back to a simple threshold‑based on/off scheme if precise timing cannot be achieved; the program must run in an infinite loop with a 200 ms pause between iterations, print the current lux reading and the computed brightness value to stdout each cycle, retry any I2C communication errors up to three times with a 100 ms delay between attempts, log an error and continue if all retries fail, and install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully release the GPIO line, close the I2C file descriptor, and turn off the LED strip before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the GPIO bus to interface a KY‑026 flame sensor (digital output, active‑low) on BCM GPIO4, a buzzer on BCM GPIO17 and an LED on BCM GPIO18, performing a startup self‑test in which the LED blinks 500 ms on/500 ms off twice while the flame sensor is read five times at 100 ms intervals, and if any of those reads indicate a persistent LOW (flame detected on all five samples) the program must signal an error by blinking the LED rapidly (100 ms on/100 ms off for five cycles) and sounding the buzzer with a short‑short‑long‑short pattern of 200 ms, 200 ms, 600 ms, 200 ms repeated three times, then exit with code 1; after a successful self‑test the main loop polls the flame sensor every 50 ms, and when a LOW is observed the buzzer and LED are turned on continuously until a subsequent read returns HIGH, at which point they are turned off, while all events (flame detected, flame cleared, any errors) are logged with timestamps; every call that requests a line or reads/writes a value must be checked and any failure handled gracefully with clear error messages, and on normal termination or receipt of SIGINT a signal handler must clean up all GPIO lines before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the ambient light from a BH1750 digital light sensor on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) once every second, stores the last 60 lux readings in a circular buffer, computes the average lux of the buffer, and blinks an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) with a 50 % duty‑cycle square wave whose frequency varies proportionally from 0.5 Hz in darkness to 5 Hz at bright levels (1000 + lux); if a sensor read fails the program must print an error, skip that sample, and attempt a new read on the next loop iteration, and on program termination via Ctrl‑C it must catch SIGINT, cleanly release the GPIO (unexport) and close the I2C file descriptor, using only standard POSIX and Linux kernel headers and no external libraries.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the GPIO bus to bit‑bang a 74HC595 shift register which drives a common‑cathode seven‑segment display, configuring GPIO17 (BCM) as the data line, GPIO18 (BCM) as the clock line, and GPIO27 (BCM) as the latch line, initializing the driver library and setting all three pins as outputs, implementing a robust shift‑out routine that sends 8 bits MSB‑first with proper clock and latch timing, mapping the 74HC595 outputs Q0 through Q7 to segments a, b, c, d, e, f, g, and dp respectively (with dp unused) so that the pattern for digit ‘5’ is shifted out, then repeatedly blinking this digit on the display with a 500 ms on period and a 500 ms off period, including error checking for the line requests and ensuring that on program exit all GPIO lines are released and the chip is cleanly closed.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads angular velocity data from a GY-50 L3G4200D gyroscope on I2C bus 1, sampling every 10 ms, converts the raw values using the 8.75 mdps/LSB sensitivity (divide by 114.285), and appends timestamped records to a file named gyro_log.csv with a header row “Timestamp,X,Y,Z” where timestamps are recorded with nanosecond precision; the program must verify that the sensor’s WHO_AM_I register returns the documented value before proceeding, retry any I2C write during initialization up to three times, check the result of every I2C call and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions appropriately, and on receipt of SIGINT perform graceful termination by closing the I2C handle, closing the CSV file, and invoking the sensor’s library cleanup API.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that drives a common‑anode RGB LED using hardware PWM at a 1 kHz frequency on the BCM pins where red is on GPIO17, green on GPIO22 and blue on GPIO27, generating a smooth color transition that reflects a simulated proximity value ranging from 0.0 to 1.0 (for example a sine‑wave function over time) rather than any external input, while handling driver library initialization errors gracefully, checking the result of every GPIO operation, and ensuring that on all exit paths—including a SIGINT interrupt—the LED is turned off and the PWM resources are released with the appropriate library call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads angular velocity from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope over the I2C bus /dev/i2c‑1 using the documented device address, with SDA connected to GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL to GPIO3 (BCM), samples the sensor every 100 ms, and appends to a file named gyro_log.txt a timestamp followed by the x, y, and z axis values in degrees per second; the program must robustly handle all I/O and I2C errors by checking the return values of open, ioctl, read and write calls and must also detect and manage the case where the sensor is absent, and it should cleanly close all file descriptors and terminate gracefully when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM, while no network logging or configuration file parsing is required.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a button wired to GPIO17 (BCM) with its internal pull‑up enabled and active‑low, debounces it with at least a 50 ms interval, and on each valid press triggers a musical doorbell by playing a stored melody from a const melody lookup table through a piezo buzzer connected to the hardware PWM0 output on GPIO18 (BCM) using the library's API call() to generate tones at a 50 % duty cycle for volume; the ISR must be non‑blocking and set a volatile flag that the main loop checks to start or, if a second press occurs during playback, gracefully stop the melody, and the program must include proper error handling for every the driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call), as well as handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by stopping PWM, releasing resources, and calling the library's API call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads edge events from an SW‑420 vibration sensor module whose digital output (active‑high) is wired to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11), using the library’s API call for edge‑triggered polling on both rising and falling edges (the same library’s API call must be invoked three times as required), accepts an optional poll timeout in milliseconds as a single command‑line argument defaulting to 1000 ms, maintains a sliding window of the last five events and, whenever three or more of those events are HIGH, prints an “EARTHQUAKE ALERT” message together with the current ISO‑8601 timestamp, logs every edge event to a persistently open file named vibration_events.log with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the raw value (0 or 1) flushing or fsyncing after each write, handles any file open or write errors gracefully by printing diagnostics to stderr without terminating, checks the return value of every driver library call and system call for errors, and installs a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, releasing the GPIO line and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads calibrated magnetic‑field data from an LSM303DLHC magnetometer connected on the I2C bus /dev/i2c‑1 using the documented 7‑bit address, with SDA wired to physical pin 3 (GPIO2/BCM) and SCL to physical pin 5 (GPIO3/BCM), samples the sensor once per second, applies the hard‑iron calibration offsets X_OFFSET = 10, Y_OFFSET = ‑5, Z_OFFSET = 20, computes a heading in degrees and maps it to one of the eight compass directions (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW), logs each sample to a file named mag_log.csv with a header row of “Timestamp, Calibrated X, Calibrated Y, Calibrated Z, Heading” if the file does not already exist and appends rows containing the timestamp, calibrated X, Y, Z values and numeric heading, prints the compass direction and numeric heading to the console, checks the result of every open, ioctl, read, write, and fopen call and, on any I2C read failure, writes a diagnostic message to stderr and skips that sample without crashing, and installs a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file and frees all resources on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM) configured with a pull‑down resistor and, on each valid touch, toggles a 5 V relay attached to GPIO17 (BCM), ensuring that touches are accepted only if at least 200 ms have elapsed since the previous one by implementing software debounce inside the interrupt service routine, logs every state change to a file named relay_log.json as a JSON object containing an ISO 8601 timestamp and the relay_state field set to “ON” or “OFF”, checks the return value of every driver library call and aborts cleanly if any call fails, and installs a SIGINT handler that, upon termination, forces the relay OFF, appends a final OFF entry to the log, invokes the required library cleanup call, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a smart irrigation system which sequentially activates four 5 V relay modules connected to GPIO17, GPIO23, GPIO24 and GPIO25 (BCM numbering) based on a simulated soil moisture value generated by rand() seeded once at startup and ranging from 0 to 100; every 10 seconds the program must obtain a new moisture reading, and if the value is below 30 it must drive each relay low (active‑low, with an inactive high level of 1) for exactly 5 seconds with a 1‑second gap between relays, appending to an irrigation_log.txt file (opened in append mode and flushed after each write) a line containing an ISO‑8601 timestamp, the relay number and the moisture level; every driver library call and file operation must be checked and any failure reported to stderr, and the program must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that deactivate all relays, release the GPIO lines, close the log file and exit cleanly, while ensuring that each GPIO line is requested as an output only once.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements an automated plant watering system using two SG90 servo motors controlled via the library's API call, with the valve servo attached to GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM) and the nozzle servo attached to GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM); the program must read a simulated soil moisture value that cycles every 1 second through the hard‑coded sequence 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 and, when the moisture is below 50, open the valve by issuing a library's API call with a pulse width corresponding to 90 degrees (≈1500 µs) then sweep the nozzle through the five angles 0, 45, 90, 135 and 180 degrees (pulse widths 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 µs) spending 2 seconds on each step, hold the spray for 5 seconds, close the valve to 0 degrees (500 µs) and then wait 5 seconds before the next cycle, while if the moisture is 50 or above the watering cycle is skipped; every library's API call must have its return value checked, be retried up to three times on failure with a 100 ms backoff and cause the program to exit on unrecoverable error, abort the watering cycle if the valve fails to open, print a critical warning if it fails to close, and log the error but continue to the next angle if a nozzle position fails; the program must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set volatile sig_atomic_t flags, and in the signal handler stop both servos by calling the library's API call with a zero argument, then invoke the library's API call cleanup function and exit cleanly, never invoking any GPIO functions before or after the library's API call in the handler; finally the code should be compiled with gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o watering watering.c -lthe driver library -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the X, Y, and Z angular velocities from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1) using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM) at the documented address, samples the data at 10 Hz, and appends each reading to a file named gyro_log.txt in CSV format containing a timestamp followed by the X, Y, and Z values; the program must check the result of every I2C system call, provide explicit handling for cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that ensure all open file descriptors and any other resources are cleanly released on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that drives a 28BYJ-48 unipolar stepper motor through an L293D driver to lock and unlock a simulated door on button press, using GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27 and GPIO22 (BCM) for the L293D IN1‑IN4 coil inputs, a LOCK button on GPIO24 (BCM) and an UNLOCK button on GPIO23 (BCM) with internal pull‑ups and active‑low logic, implementing full‑step (single‑coil) excitation and rotating the motor 512 steps clockwise for a LOCK press and 512 steps counter‑clockwise for an UNLOCK press with a 3 ms inter‑step delay, debouncing the button reads so a single press does not trigger multiple rotations, de‑energizing all coils after each rotation to reduce power consumption and heating, printing console messages for lock, unlock and any errors, checking the return value of the library’s API call() after every operation and reporting an error on failure, and handling SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) gracefully by de‑energizing the coils and calling the library’s API call() before exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (64‑bit, Bookworm) that reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor and logs the result every second to a file named distance_log.txt opened in append mode and kept open for the lifetime of the program; the trigger line must be requested as an output on GPIO17 (BCM) and the echo line as an input on GPIO18 (BCM) with active‑high polarity, the sensor’s 5 V echo output being reduced to 3.3 V by a voltage divider or level shifter before reaching the Pi, the program must generate a 10 µs trigger pulse, wait for the rising edge of the echo with a 50 ms timeout, then wait for the falling edge with the same timeout, compute the distance, and write the value to the log, pausing at least 60 ms between measurements and sampling at a 1 s interval; on any timeout or driver call failure the program must write “‑1” to the file and print an error message to stderr, and any GPIO initialisation failure must be reported to stderr, while SIGINT or SIGTERM must be caught to cleanly release all driver resources and close the log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads distance from a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor attached to I2C bus 1 using the documented default address, polls the sensor every 100 ms, prints the current distance to stdout, and drives a relay connected to GPIO18 (BCM) so that the relay is set HIGH when the measured distance is less than or equal to 50 cm and LOW otherwise, while checking every driver and I2C return value, handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error by logging all such errors to stderr, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT the program cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C interface, setting the relay pin low, and terminating the driver usage.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the angular velocity from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope over the hardware I2C bus /dev/i2c‑1 using the documented device address, with SDA connected to GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL to GPIO3 (BCM); the program must continuously acquire the x, y, and z axis rotation rates and log those three values to the console, while checking the result of every I2C read and write system call and handling any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and it must also install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that all resources are cleanly released on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements an automated plant watering system by sequentially activating four 5 V relay modules connected to GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27 and GPIO22 (BCM numbers, physical pins 11, 12, 13, 15); the program must open the library’s API, request all four lines as outputs with active‑low semantics, set all lines HIGH (inactive) at startup, then in a main loop that polls every 60 seconds activate each relay in turn for exactly 5 seconds, repeating the whole sequence once every 86 400 seconds (24 hours) beginning immediately on launch, log the start time of each full cycle to a file named watering_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS”, check the result of every library call and every file I/O operation handling errors including the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that releases all GPIO lines, closes the chip and exits cleanly; the code must be compiled with gcc ‑o watering watering.c ‑lgpiod and must not use any deprecated driver interface.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that creates a smart lighting sunrise effect by gradually increasing the intensity of four SRD-05VDC relay modules over a 30‑minute period, stepping the change every second and using a 1 kHz hardware PWM signal with duty cycles from 0 to 255 applied simultaneously to the relays connected to GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27 and GPIO22 (BCM numbering, equivalent to wiringPi pins 0, 1, 2, 3); the program must log every event with timestamps to a file named smart_lighting.log, verify each GPIO pin mode setup and check the library’s API call() return values, handle any PWM initialization failures gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads angular velocity from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, with SDA connected to GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL to GPIO3 (BCM), sampling at 20 Hz (a 50 ms period), storing each timestamped X, Y, and Z reading in a 100‑entry in‑memory circular buffer, continuously checking every driver call for errors, printing an error and exiting if I2C initialization fails, and if a read fails attempting re‑initialization up to three times before exiting; the program must drive an LED on GPIO17 (BCM) such that the LED is turned on whenever the absolute value of any axis exceeds 250 deg/s and turned off when all axes are below that threshold, without configuring the accelerometer, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle, setting the LED GPIO low, and invoking the library’s cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the X, Y, and Z angular rates from an MPU‑9250 gyroscope over SPI and logs them to a CSV file named gyro_log.txt; the SPI bus to use is /dev/spidev0.0 configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, 8 bits per word, MSB first, with manual chip select on CE0 implemented via libgpiod on /dev/gpiochip0 line offset 8 (GPIO8, BCM), asserting the chip‑select line low during each transfer and de‑asserting it high otherwise, performing a read every 10 ms and retrying up to three times on any SPI communication error, writing each record as an ISO 8601 timestamp with nanosecond resolution followed by the three rate values in CSV format (timestamp,x_rate,y_rate,z_rate), handling persistent SPI failures by logging an error to stderr and continuing, handling file write errors gracefully, performing proper error checking on all system and library calls, and cleaning up the SPI device, GPIO line, and closing the log file when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM, while running indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the X‑axis angular rate from an Analog Devices ADXRS290 dual‑axis MEMS gyroscope over hardware SPI0 configured at 1 MHz, mode 0 (CPOL = 0, CPHA = 0) using CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) as chip‑enable, SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO9 (BCM); the program must set the MSB (bit 7) of the register address to 1 for a read, transmit the address, then read the data payload, timestamp each reading with clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) and store it in a thread‑safe in‑memory circular buffer of capacity 100 entries, continuously monitor the measured rate against a threshold of 20.0 deg/s turning a warning LED on GPIO17 (BCM) on when the threshold is exceeded and off when it falls back below, check the return values of all driver library initialization and SPI transfer calls, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM exit gracefully by closing the SPI interface, turning off the LED, terminating the driver library and releasing all resources.
